name: Stern–Gerlach (1922)
description: Stern and Gerlach sent silver atoms through a strongly non-uniform magnetic field. The atoms are neutral, but each carries a tiny magnetic moment, whose energy $-\mathbf{m}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ changes where the field changes: the beam split in two, one part for each spin state. Here the two spin states fly as two shots. Place a magnet so that each reaches its own detector: one state is pushed towards stronger field, the other away (see the magnetic map).

reality.represents: The Stern–Gerlach experiment (1922): spin splits a beam in two

remarks.line: The force of a field gradient
remarks.detail: A neutral particle with a magnetic moment feels no Lorentz force, only the pull of the field's gradient, m ∇B_z, as the silver atoms did.

Each state flies as its own shot, its moment fixed along z. In quantum mechanics each atom is in a superposition, and the field picks one of two outcomes: the splitting into exactly two beams is the quantum part, put in by hand here.
Stern and Gerlach used an electromagnet with a knife-edge pole over a grooved one for a strong gradient; the beams split by a fraction of a millimetre. A spherical magnet's dipole field here.
The atoms came from an oven with a broad spread of speeds, which smeared each beam; here each state has one speed.
